facts.text: The white-throated needletail is reputed to reach speeds of up to 170 km/h in horizontal flight, though this remains unverified.
facts.quote: It is reputed to reach speeds of up to 170 km/h (110 mph) in horizontal flight, but this is unverified because the methods used to measure its speed have not been published.

facts.text: A likelier cruising speed is 75 km/h, which is still at least 100 times the bird's body length per second.
facts.quote: 75 km/h (47 mph) is more likely, but this is still at least 100 times the bird's length per second.

facts.text: It nests in rock crevices in cliffs or in hollow trees.
facts.quote: They build their nests in rock crevices in cliffs or hollow trees.

facts.text: The white-throated needletail spends most of its time in the air and dislikes sitting on the ground.
facts.quote: They do not like to sit on the ground and spend most of their time in the air.

facts.text: It feeds on small flying insects, including beetles, flies, bees and moths.
facts.quote: They feed on small, flying insects like beetles, flies, bees and moths.

facts.text: The white-throated needletail migrates, breeding in Central Asia and southern Siberia and wintering in places including Australia.
facts.quote: The white-throated needletail is a migratory bird, breeding in Central Asia and southern Siberia, and wintering south in the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and Australia.

facts.text: It is about 20 cm long, weighs 110 to 120 grams, and has a robust, barrel-like body.
facts.quote: White-throated needletails are large swifts with a robust, barrel-like body. They measure about 20 cm (7.9 in) and weigh between 110 and 120 grams (3.9 and 4.2 oz).

facts.text: It is greyish-brown with a white throat and a white patch running from the base of the tail to the flanks.
facts.quote: They are greyish-brown except for a white throat and a white patch, extending from the base of the tail to the flanks.

facts.text: The needletail is named for the spined end of its tail, which is not forked like the tails of typical swifts.
facts.quote: Needle-tailed swifts get their name from the spined end of their tail, which is not forked as it is in the typical swifts of the genus Apus.

facts.text: In 2013 a needletail seen in Great Britain for the first time in 22 years later died after flying into a wind turbine, and its body went to a museum.
facts.quote: In June 2013, an individual was spotted in Great Britain for the first time in 22 years. It later flew into a wind turbine and died; its body was sent to a museum.
